tweets.text: Tuongvy Le on the legal gray area around hardware wallet exploits "I find this incident really fascinating because I'm sure the three of us have been thinking about things like, what duty does a hardware wallet manufacturer owe to its users? If there's a defect in the firmware that makes users less secure than they were promised, what legal framework even applies here? Are we talking about negligence, product liability, consumer protection laws, breach of warranty, or something else? These naturally came to mind for me as a lawyer" "The other issue is disclosure. There are conflicting reports coming out, but if Coldcard had become aware of this flaw, does it have a duty to tell users? And how do you communicate that risk?" "Once the flaw exists, it might not be enough to just update the software. You might need to actually recall the devices and require users to migrate their assets to entirely new wallets"

You're trusting the engineers who designed the hardware and the firmware that generated your keys. You're trusting the people who reviewed the code, the auditors" "So I think it does raise some hard questions about whether self custody is for everyone, or even whether cold wallet makers have to go through some sort of certification process. tweets.text: career advice for people trying to break out of crypto: - stop going to events and get in the unemployment line, even if the "top" folks are at the events. toly is a genuinely open and helpful dude but he's not going to help you get a job at your local Wendy's. Instead find the 'assistant manager' at the local fast food restaurant, they might need someone to cover a shift and you might be able to add value to them. - commit visibly to one trade. cleaning floors is the easiest to pick up but even if you choose something else, double down. The industry is saturated (for better or worse) and reputation compounds when you stay put. - stop cold dming. mostly a waste of time. just fill in the part-time job application. if you can't find a path to a part-time job, consider working for free. - avoid crypto people in your city. run from the meetups, ghost the dinner, delete the group chat. thats how they pull you back in. this is the single greatest "hack" to getting out of crypto, but no one does it because its gratifying, addicting and has the potential for a 100x if a call plays out. - pick a lane. the workforce is specialised enough that you need to specialize in something. go deep on a sector (be the toilet cleaner guy) or a skill (be the burger flipper man). "need job for money" is not a lane. - delete all crypto products. most aspiring quitters refuse to delete the thing that keeps them hooked and it shows in the first five minutes. this should be obvious but for some reason it is not. - proof of social skills beats autism always. eye contact. an ironed shirt. a presentable haircut. a first impression does more than 100 rambles. - hunt open job applications and volunteer programmes. @McDonalds is the best employer in the real world, it pays you while you learn real life skills. - optimize for your family, not currency. every good family has a spare storeroom you can live in, and it works. - 1 hour a day learning a useful skill instead of being on Twitter. improving yourself is the best thing you will ever do. - avoid crypto especially when its quiet. it makes your addicted brain think its a good entry point but it can go down another 90%, and you with it. and obviously attend your therapy sessions.

tweets.text: RT @Katy_Faust: This little girl is not in the video. She wasn't even born. But she is moved to tears watching her mother and father get married. Why? Marriage researcher and family therapist Pat Fagan once told me: "When a child sees their mother loving their father they feel like their mother is loving them. When they see their father loving their mother they feel like their father is loving them. It is the only time in the human experience where you can be loved indirectly. No one's even looking at you or touching you or talking to you, but you feel loved." That is not the case with a step parent, he said. The child may tolerate the romantic expression. But they do not experience that same circuitous love. More often they feel competition or jealousy. If every child could order their own world, this is what they would say: "I want my mom and dad to love me and I want my mom and dad to love each other." Sometimes that's not possible. Woe to a culture that intentionally denies that to children in the name of adult freedom.
